Positioning and Design Philosophy: SLA Is Not a Rust Clone

This page answers the most common first question: what exactly is the relationship between SLA and Rust? The conclusion up front — SLA is not a simplified version or clone of Rust, but one of many high-level frontends for the SA platform. After reading this page, you will be able to judge which language suits the project at hand, and know which expectations need correcting when you bring Rust experience over.

NoteThe data in this chapter is taken from docs/rust_vs_sla_final_cn.md (v0.2 corrected edition, 2026-06-15) and the surface compatibility assessment report from the same day. It is a point-in-time snapshot: percentages, multiples, and phase divisions reflect the measurements and plans at that time, not permanent guarantees.

One-Sentence Conclusion

Rust is a “full-featured systems language + large native ecosystem + mature toolchain”; SLA is an “LLM-friendly frontend for SA + WASM speed optimization + zero-trust package management + bc2sa multi-language ecosystem bridge”. SLA is not a Rust replacement.

Positioning Differences

DimensionRustSLA
Design goalSystems-level safe language + general-purpose applicationsLLM/tool-friendly high-level frontend for SA
Primary usersSystems engineers, application developersLLM Agents, the SA toolchain, ECS / WASM scenarios
Lower-level outputProduces LLVM IR directlyProduces SA IR → LLVM-C → wasm/native
How the ecosystem is enteredInternal crates.io ecosystembc2sa bridges the full Rust/C++/C/Swift/Zig ecosystem + native SLA packages
CategoryGeneral-purpose programming languageOne of many frontends for the SA platform
Ecosystem maturity10+ years, 130K+ cratesIndirectly inherits the Rust/C++ ecosystem via bc2sa; native SLA is about 6 months old

Key point: when you evaluate SLA you must count the platform it sits on — it is the combination of SA high-level frontend + bc2sa bridge, not an isolated language. bc2sa is an LLVM bitcode → SA translation channel that lets SLA indirectly call the results of any language that can produce LLVM bitcode (currently a restricted subset; see the source document snapshot for coverage figures).

Forks in Design Philosophy

Both do memory safety, but by different implementation paths:

  • Explicit ownership symbols: SA's five-symbol contract is = & ^ ! *. On the SLA user surface you mainly encounter two of them: &x creates a borrowed view, ^x explicitly transfers ownership; ! (release) is implicitly injected by the compiler and is not written by the user. Rust, by contrast, uses implicit move plus the Drop trait.
  • No cross-function lifetime inference: Rust forces 'a annotations; SLA parses but discards them, and cross-function borrowing safety follows a “frontend responsibility” model.
  • Read/write are not distinguished at the syntax level: Rust distinguishes them with &T/&mut T; SLA has only &, decided dynamically by the SA Referee (see the Ownership and Borrowing: Referee vs the Borrow Checker page).
  • An extremely small verifier: Rust's borrow-checking-related code is about 200K lines; the SA Referee targets ≤2500 lines and can be formally proven (Coq / FPGA programming is on the roadmap).
  • Zero-trust package management: sa pkg uses URL-based decentralized namespaces, SHA-256 pinning, module-level grants permission ledgers, a strict ban on binary distribution, and built-in X-ray scanning and tribunal-based rights confirmation; cargo uses a centralized SemVer + process-level permission model.
// Rust：赋值即隐式 move
let a = make_value();
let b = a;            // a 的所有权悄悄转给 b
// 此后再用 a 会编译报错

// Sla：转移写在源码里
let a = make_value();
let b = ^a;           // ^ 前缀显式声明 move
// 此后再用 a 得到 UseAfterMove 编译错误

Capabilities Exclusive to Each

Exclusive to Rust

  • 130K+ crates native ecosystem; first-tier IDE experience with rust-analyzer
  • Production-grade async runtime (tokio); full proc-macro + macro_rules!
  • Cross-function lifetime inference; full trait coherence solving
  • Mature multi-platform binary distribution; ten years of production validation; unified style with rustfmt + clippy; rich teaching resources

Exclusive to SLA

  • WASM compilation speed (early target 10-20×) and output size (early target about 5× smaller); measured on 2026-10-22: the compilation speed target was not met, and with both sides in their size-optimal configurations typical WASM loads are about 5× smaller (matmul is an exception), see the SLA vs Rust vs Go Performance Measurements (native / WASM / compilation / networking) page; O(1) borrow checking
  • Verifier can be formally proven / programmed onto FPGA (roadmap); built-in Gas metering
  • Zero-trust package management (grants module-level ledger), tribunal + stained CI, airlock FFI (function-level isolation)
  • Minimal keyword set: no lifetime annotations, no Send/Sync, no coherence solving
  • LLM self-repair loop (native structured JSON Traps); bc2sa multi-language ecosystem bridge; multi-frontend architecture
NoteMeasurements on 2026-10-22 corrected the old framing: in Release mode, Rust's native/WASM runtime medians are about 1.47×/1.44× faster respectively (excluding the matmul outlier), Rust is faster for cold compilation of conventional source code; for hot compilation Rust is still faster on large source code, but the gap disappears or even reverses on small WASM projects; but with both sides in their size-optimal configurations, typical SLA WASM is about 1/5 the size of Rust's (matmul is an exception, where SLA is instead about 1.76×). See the SLA vs Rust vs Go Performance Measurements (native / WASM / compilation / networking) page for details.

Which to Choose by Scenario

ScenarioRecommendation
Desktop applications, heavy Web backends, OS/drivers, large multi-person collaboration projects, need for a mature IDERust
Need production-grade frameworks such as tokio / serde / bevy / wgpuRust
WASM edge computing, WASM games, embedded WASM/IoT displays (size is usually an advantage, but you need to check the CPU/latency budget)SLA
LLM sandboxes / Agent execution environments, teaching, educational ECS (sa3d), safety/aviation (provable Referee)SLA
Want to reuse an existing Rust/C++ crate and deploy to WASM (need to measure whether the size is acceptable)bc2sa bridging + SLA calls

Points That Are Easily Misunderstood

Common claimReality
“SLA is a simplified version of Rust”No. SLA is a high-level frontend for SA, at a different abstraction layer from Rust
“The SLA ecosystem has to be built from 0 over several years”bc2sa lets SLA consume the Rust/C++ ecosystem; see the source document snapshot for the coverage improvement roadmap
“SLA is compatible with Rust syntax”Only at the surface (Phase 1 about 70%). The semantic layer is always different: reversed mutability, &self covers read and write, no proc-macro
“SLA is faster than Rust”Not true. Rust release is faster on most loads; SLA leads only in a few scenarios such as sort/hashmap. See the SLA vs Rust vs Go Performance Measurements (native / WASM / compilation / networking) page
“SLA's async cannot be used”async/await has been measured to run (tests/test_unit_async_await.sla); what is missing is a tokio-equivalent runtime ecosystem
“SLA has no incremental compilation”SA incremental compilation has landed (sci/src/cli.zig)
“SLA has no DCE”DCE at the SA layer has landed (commit 146c7db)

Key Points of This Page

  • SLA and Rust are two different things at different abstraction layers: one is a high-level frontend for the SA platform, the other is a general-purpose systems language.
  • The ecosystem gap is narrowed by bc2sa bridging, not by rewriting.
  • Performance is not an across-the-board SLA advantage: measured runtime and compilation time are worse than Rust release; WASM size has the advantage on typical loads with both sides in their size-optimal configurations (about 1/5), but matmul is an exception, and native size is still about 33×.
  • The next page looks at how much the concrete syntax differs: Syntax Comparison Matrix (Measured); for an item-by-item comparison of memory safety see the Ownership and Borrowing: Referee vs the Borrow Checker page; for differences in macros and metaprogramming see the Macros and Metaprogramming Compared page; for full benchmark data see the SLA vs Rust vs Go Performance Measurements (native / WASM / compilation / networking) page.
